# NS-3 network-level validation — aggregated results

**Tasks:** T-N1 – T-N7 (`NS3-Simulation.md`) · **Generated by:** `scripts/ns3_experiments/aggregate_results.py` from **29** saved raw runs in `reports/ns3_runs/`

> ## Provenance of every number in this report
> **Every latency, delay, jitter, throughput and detection count below is NS-3 SIMULATION OUTPUT.** None of it is a physical measurement. Specifically:
> - **No Raspberry Pi number appears anywhere in this report.** `Build-Instructions.md` T4.3's hardware benchmark does not exist yet — `src/deployment/benchmark.py` refuses to produce one off the target device — so the headline comparison `NS3-Simulation.md` T-N3 asks for **cannot be run**, and no run here is labelled as this project's architecture on real hardware.
> - **No base-paper latency appears anywhere either.** The base paper reports no per-flow inference latency at all (`PRD.md §2.2`), so there is nothing to plug in and nothing was invented. Every `--idsLatencyUs` below is a **swept sensitivity value**.
> - A simulated `mean end-to-end delay` models what would happen at network scale. It is not a substitute for T4.3 and must never be quoted as one (`NS3-Simulation.md §A.1`).

See [`docs/latency_provenance.md`](../docs/latency_provenance.md) for the full trace.

## 1. What was simulated (T-N1)

The `20 wearables / 60 compromised` phrasing `NS3-Simulation.md §A.1` flags as ambiguous is resolved by construction: these are **three disjoint node sets**, never subsets.

| Role | Count | Behaviour |
|---|---:|---|
| wearables (legitimate) | 20 | periodic telemetry, 600 ms period, 40% seeded jitter |
| attacker-bots | 60 | flood at 5 ms; in T-N5 half switch to a 450 ms slow-and-low wave |
| fog nodes (IDS) | 4 | single-server queue, one flow per `idsLatencyUs` |

Fog IDS capacity is printed **both per-node and aggregate** in every run, which settles the other ambiguity `§B.2` raises: per-node capacity is `1e6/idsLatencyUs`, aggregate is `nFog x` that.

## 2. The congestion-coupled detector goes blind — in both directions (T-N2)

`NS3-Simulation.md §B.1` describes a prior `C_batched` run with 0 alerts and 0/60 blocked, and hypothesises that a fog node fast enough to avoid queue buildup never produces the timing signature the rule reacts to. **That prior run does not exist in this repository** — there was no `scratch/hids-iomt-adaptive.cc` to inventory, in the working tree or in git history — so nothing here is a reproduction of it. What follows establishes the mechanism from scratch, on this project's own reconstruction of a congestion-adaptive rule.

The rule keys its threshold to fog-node queue occupancy. There are only two ways to couple them, and **each is blind at one end of the load range**:

| Coupling | tau | IDS latency | max load | min tau reached | Alerts | Attackers blocked |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| inverse | 500·(1−load) | 57.9 µs | 0.0150 | 492.5 ms | 216 | 60/60 |
| inverse | 500·(1−load) | 14542.7 µs | 0.9950 | 2.5 ms | 8 | 0/60 |
| direct | 500·load | 57.9 µs | 0.0150 | 0.0 ms | 156 | 45/60 |
| direct | 500·load | 14542.7 µs | 0.9950 | 0.0 ms | 894 | 60/60 |

**The mechanism is confirmed, and it is not a bug.** A threshold multiplied by a load term collapses to zero at one end of that term's range, and no inter-message gap can be shorter than zero. Under `inverse`, a **congested** fog node stops alerting (8 alerts, 0/60 blocked) — the detector fails exactly when the network is under attack hard enough to saturate it. Under `direct`, a **fast** fog node under-detects (45/60 blocked against 60/60 when congested), which is the direction `§B.2` hypothesised.

This is a property of *coupling detection sensitivity to congestion at all*, not of either particular sign. A rule of this shape is a **congestion detector wearing an intrusion detector's label** — which is a fair fifth objection to the base paper's family of adjacency-table timing rules, and is reported as this project's own finding about its own reconstruction, not as a claim about anyone's published code.

## 3. Three threshold rules, same scenario (T-N4)

All at `idsLatencyUs=500` (swept), 60 attacker-bots, 20 wearables, 30 simulated seconds.

| Rule | Alerts | True positives | **False positives** | Attackers blocked | **Wearables blocked (FP)** |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `fixed` | 327 | 267 | **60** | 60/60 | **20/20** |
| `ewma` | 303 | 267 | **36** | 60/60 | **8/20** |
| `criticality` | 296 | 267 | **29** | 60/60 | **9/20** |

Three distinct outcomes, so the criticality rule is demonstrably not a no-op (T-N4's VERIFY). The `fixed` row is the base paper's flat τ = 500 ms, and it is the reason Objection #4 exists: it blocks **every legitimate wearable in the simulation**. A rule that quarantines the entire patient-monitoring estate has not detected an intrusion, it has caused one.

## 4. The `PRD.md §3.1` >30% false-positive-reduction target

- False-positive **alerts**: 60 (fixed) → 29 (criticality) = **-51.7%**
- Falsely **blocked wearables**: 20 (fixed) → 9 (criticality) = **-55.0%**

**Answer: YES on this simulated quantity — and the target is still not met.**

Both reductions clear 30% *in the simulation*, but this **does not** satisfy `PRD.md §3.1`, and reporting it as though it did would be the exact substitution `NS3-Simulation.md §A.1` rule 4 forbids. The PRD's target is a false-positive reduction **on unseen attack types, by the trained ensemble, against the leakage-free baseline**. That quantity is measured in [`reports/t3_4_adaptive_threshold.md`](t3_4_adaptive_threshold.md), where the best measured reduction is **−10.8%** and the target is **not met**.

What this section measures is a different thing that happens to share a name: how many *legitimate devices a timing rule quarantines* in a simulated network. A rule can be excellent at that and still leave the ensemble's false-positive rate untouched, because the two decisions are made by different components on different evidence. **The PRD target remains unmet; this is corroborating evidence for the criticality weighting, not a substitute measurement.**

## 5. Sensitivity to IDS inspection cost (swept — no measured value exists)

| Rule | 57.9 µs | 500 µs | 2000 µs | 14542.7 µs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fixed` | 240 alerts, 60/60 | 327 alerts, 60/60 | 1025 alerts, 60/60 | 1036 alerts, 60/60 |
| `ewma` | 216 alerts, 60/60 | 303 alerts, 60/60 | 102 alerts, 0/60 | 8 alerts, 0/60 |
| `criticality` | 209 alerts, 60/60 | 296 alerts, 60/60 | 994 alerts, 60/60 | 1000 alerts, 60/60 |

Reported as *alerts, attackers blocked*. The 57.9 µs and 14542.7 µs columns are the two values named in `NS3-Simulation.md §B.1`; they are carried forward **only** as sweep points, since §B.2 records that their own origin was never established.

### Three different things called "dropped"

| Rule | latency | reached fog | queue overflow (loss) | source blocked (success) | network loss | mean delay (sim) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `fixed` | 500 µs | 336,952 | 0 (0.0%) | 336,410 (99.8%) | 0.0128% | 3.0828 ms |
| `fixed` | 14542.7 µs | 336,952 | 8,285 (2.5%) | 327,393 (97.2%) | 0.0128% | 3.0828 ms |
| `criticality` | 500 µs | 336,952 | 0 (0.0%) | 336,012 (99.7%) | 0.0128% | 3.0828 ms |
| `criticality` | 14542.7 µs | 336,952 | 8,285 (2.5%) | 327,029 (97.1%) | 0.0128% | 3.0828 ms |

Three columns, three meanings, and collapsing them into one "packet loss" figure would misrepresent all three:

- **queue overflow** — the IDS could not keep up. A genuine failure, and the cost of a slow inspection path.
- **source blocked** — the IDS already decided this source was hostile and is refusing its traffic. This is the system **working**, and it dominates the totals precisely because blocking works: a blocked bot keeps flooding and keeps being refused.
- **network loss** — what FlowMonitor sees on the wire. Everything above already arrived.

### Why the simulated delay does not move with IDS cost

`mean end-to-end delay` is identical across every row above, and that is a **limitation of this model, not a result**. IDS service time is modelled inside the fog application's own queue; it is not a `NetDevice` transmission queue, so FlowMonitor — which measures the wire — never sees it. The delay column therefore reports network transit only. **The detection-latency question this layer cannot answer is exactly the one T4.3's Raspberry Pi benchmark exists to answer**, which is another reason nothing here substitutes for it.

## 7. Incremental-learning stand-in (T-N5)

**NS-3 cannot retrain a model.** The stand-in is a threshold change at t = 20 s representing a model that has absorbed a new attack type; a novel *slow-and-low* wave (450 ms period, deliberately just under the base paper's flat 500 ms) starts at t = 10 s. Full reasoning in [`docs/incremental_scenario.md`](../docs/incremental_scenario.md).

| Rule | Update | Alerts before | Alerts after | FP before | FP after | Attackers blocked |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `fixed` | none | 282 | 0 | 60 | 0 | 60/60 |
| `fixed` | applied | 282 | 0 | 60 | 0 | 60/60 |
| `criticality` | none | 160 | 1 | 28 | 1 | 30/60 |
| `criticality` | applied | 160 | 121 | 28 | 31 | 60/60 |

The criticality rule's update takes attacker blocking from **30/60 to 60/60** — it catches the slow-and-low wave the un-updated rule misses. It is **not free**: false-positive alerts rise from 28 to 31 in the after-phase, because a threshold loosened enough to catch a 450 ms attacker also catches more jittery telemetry. That trade is the finding, and reporting the detection gain without it would be dishonest.

The `fixed` rule shows no before/after difference at all: its flat 500 ms already blocks all 60 bots in the before-phase, leaving nothing for an update to improve. A rule with one constant has nothing to adapt.

## 8. What this layer does not establish

- **No hardware number.** T-N3's headline comparison is blocked on the same Raspberry Pi that blocks `Build-Instructions.md` T4.2/T4.3. Until that exists, this layer answers "how does the *rule* behave at network scale", never "how fast is it".
- **The detector here is a timing rule, not the ensemble.** No CNN/BiLSTM/Transformer runs inside NS-3. Detection outcomes above are the adaptive-threshold contribution's behaviour, not the ensemble's accuracy.
- **The EWMA rule is this project's reconstruction**, built to have the shape §B.2 describes. Its failure modes are real properties of that shape; they are not evidence about any specific published implementation.
- **Single seed (42), single run number**, as everywhere else in this project.

## 9. Reproducing

```bash
scripts/ns3_experiments/run_matrix.sh [path-to-ns-3-dev]   # writes reports/ns3_runs/
python scripts/ns3_experiments/aggregate_results.py         # writes this report
```

Raw runs aggregated here: **29**. Every table above is re-derivable from them.
